Introduction Several rodent-borne hantaviruses are recognized as important human pathogens causing hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) primarily in Asia and Europe, and hantavirus pulmonary syndrome (HPS) in the Americas, which are mainly acquired through the inhalation of infectious respiratory particles from rodent urine or feces. The viruses are distributed globally, and approximately 200,000 cases are reported annually, posing a persistent threat to human health [1]. In China, Hantaan virus (HTNV) and Seoul virus (SEOV) are the causative agents of HFRS, and the infection has a relatively wide distribution, with the highest annual reported cases exceeding 110000 in 1980s [2]. Although the annual incidence of HFRS had significantly decreased and maintained a low level in the last two decades, the geographical distribution range of Hantavirus (HV) infection had shown an expanding trend, and the virus presents a more abundant genetic diversity [3]. HV are predominantly hosted by rodents and exhibit strict host specificity, each hantavirus species is primarily carried and transmitted by one or several closely related reservoir hosts [4]. Virus–host adaptive evolution is influenced by ecological environments, host switching events, and gene selection pressures, contributing to the genetic diversity of hantaviruses. Moreover, as segmented RNA viruses, HV possess the capacity for genetic reassortment, enabling the exchange of genomic segments between two parental viruses co-infecting the same cell, thereby generating progeny viruses genetically distinct from both parents [5]. The frequency of segment exchange and the co-infection rate within the same host cell affect the success of genomic reassortment [6]. With the rapid development of laboratory testing technology and the expansion of pathogen monitoring scope, new HV strains continued to be discovered, presenting rich genetic diversity with regional characteristics in China [3,7]. It has been demonstrated that immunization with HFRS bivalent inactivated vaccine (HFRSbiv) which contains HTNV and SEOV, was an effective measure for HFRS prevention. HFRSbiv targeting HTNV and SEOV had been licensed for over two decades. Combined with comprehensive interventions such as immunization, rodent control and environmental sanitation, the disease burden of HFRS in China has been significantly reduced [8,9]. However, the vaccine strains used in China (e.g., HTNV PS-6, SD9805, and SEOV L99, HB9908) were isolated more than 20 years ago. Antigenic variation may exist among different strains within the same serotype, and its impact on vaccine protective efficacy remains unclear. Therefore, evaluating the immunogenicity of regional epidemic HV strains, as well as the immunogenic matching and cross-protection between vaccine strains and currently circulating strains, is practically important. In this study, a serum panel was established using serum samples collected from confirmed HFRS patients and HFRS vaccinees for a comparative analysis of the immunogenicity of HV circulating in China and vaccine strains using an enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay-based microneutralization test (MN-ELISA). The neutralizing antibody levels against vaccine strains and representative epidemic strains were systematically compared to elucidate immunogenicity differences and to provide experimental evidence for the scientific evaluation of the protective efficacy of HFRS vaccine. Materials and methods Ethics statement This study received ethics approval from the Ethical Committee of National Institute for Viral Disease Control and Prevention, Chinese Center for Disease Control and Prevention. Written informed consent was obtained from all participants. Study subjects A total of 48 convalescent serum samples from HFRS patients and 28 serum samples from individuals who had completed a three-dose regimen with HFRSbiv were collected between 2019 and 2020 from Heilongjiang Province, which belonged to HFRS national surveillance system. The median interval between disease onset and serum collection for HFRS patients was 14 days, with an interquartile range (IQR) of 10.5 to 19.5 days. Serum samples from vaccinees were collected within one month after the third (booster) dose. HV amplification and titration The HTNV vaccine strain 84FLi, SEOV vaccine strain L99, and previously isolated epidemic strains SX26, LN03, and FJ-17 from HFRS national surveillance system were selected for neutralization assays. All strains were propagated in Vero-E6 cells prior to use. Viral replication was confirmed by quantitative real-time reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction (qRT-PCR) and indirect immunofluorescence assay (IFA). Viral titers were determined by plaque assay. Virus resuscitation, propagation, and identification. HV vaccine strains (84FLi, L99) and epidemic strains (SX26, LN03, FJ-17) were thawed on ice and used to infect Vero-E6 cells. Culture supernatants were collected on day 7 post-infection for HV nucleic acid detection by qRT-PCR. Concurrently, cell antigen slides were prepared for IFA. Plaque assay for viral titration. Vero-E6 cells cultured for 24 h were seeded into 6-well plates and incubated overnight at 37°C with 5% CO2. After forming confluent monolayer, the monolayers were washed, and 500 μL of MEM maintenance medium was added to each well. Serial 10-fold dilutions (10−1 to 10−5) of virus stocks were prepared in MEM, and 500 μL of each dilution was inoculated per well in duplicate. Plates were incubated at 37°C, 5% CO2 for 1.5–2 h for adsorption. After removal of the inoculum, 3 mL of pre-warmed (42°C) agarose overlay (mainly 2 x MEM containing 10% fetal bovine serum,2% Gibco HEPES,1% Penicillin-Streptomycin and 2% low-melting-point agarose) was added per well. Once solidified, plates were inverted and incubated at 37°C, 5% CO2. Seven days later, a second agarose overlay, which was identical to that of the first overlay, with the addition of 3% neutral red to facilitate plaque visualization, was added, and incubation continued for an additional 48–72 h. Plaques were observed and counted. Viral titers were calculated as plaque-forming units per milliliter (PFU/mL): PFU/mL = (average plaque count at a given dilution × reciprocal of dilution) / virus inoculum volume (mL/well). Detection of serum HV IgG antibodies HV IgG antibodies in all serum samples were detected using a commercial HV IgG antibody ELISA kit (Beijing Beier Bioengineering Co., Ltd., enzyme immunoassay). Positive and negative controls were included. All procedures and result interpretation were performed strictly in accordance with the manufacturer’s instructions. Neutralizing antibody assay (MN-ELISA) A fixed-virus (100 PFU/0.1 mL) microneutralization assay was employed. Sera were heat-inactivated at 56°C and serially diluted 2-fold in 96-well plates (starting dilution 1:10 for vaccinees and 1:20 for patients, ending at 1:10240), with three replicates per dilution. Each virus strain (84FLi, L99, SX26, LN03, FJ-17) was diluted to working concentration, and 50 μL of virus was mixed with an equal volume of diluted serum. The mixtures were incubated at 37°C, 5% CO2 for 1 h. Subsequently, 100 μL of Vero-E6 cell suspension was added to each well. Virus-positive and cell-negative controls were included. After seven days of incubation at 37°C, 5% CO2, supernatants were discarded, and cells were fixed with cold acetone and inactivated under UV light. After washing, 100 μL of detection antibody mixture (HV monoclonal antibody L13F3 at 1:3200 dilution and HRP-conjugated rabbit anti-mouse IgG at 1:1000 dilution, pre-mixed) was added per well and incubated at 37°C for 45 min. After washing, 100 μL of the mixed TMB substrate solution was added to each well and incubated for 10 min at room temperature in the dark. The reaction was stopped by adding 50 μL of 2 M H2SO4 per well, and the optical density (OD) was measured at 450 nm using a microplate reader. Determination of neutralizing antibody titer and virus typing The neutralizing antibody titer was defined as the highest serum dilution that inhibited 50% of viral infection. The cutoff value (X) for positivity was calculated as: X = [(mean OD of cell-positive controls – mean OD of cell-negative controls)/2) + mean OD of cell-negative controls [10]. Samples with OD values below X were considered positive for neutralization, and the reciprocal of the highest dilution showing positivity was taken as the neutralizing antibody titer. For virus typing, the neutralizing antibody titers against the HTNV vaccine strain 84FLi and the SEOV vaccine strain L99 were compared. If the titer against one type was ≥ 4-fold higher than that against the other, the infection was assigned to that type; otherwise, it was considered untypable. Statistical analysis Raw data were entered, organized, and analyzed using Excel 2019 and GraphPad Prism 10.1.2. Neutralizing antibody titers were expressed as geometric mean titer (GMT). Comparisons among multiple groups were performed using one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA). For non-normally distributed data, non-parametric tests (Wilcoxon signed-rank test for two-group comparisons, Friedman test for paired multiple-group comparisons) were applied. A P-value < 0.05 was considered statistically significant. Results HV amplification and titer determination To obtain working virus stocks for subsequent neutralization assays, five HV strains (vaccine strains: 84FLi, L99; epidemic strains: SX26, LN03, FJ-17) were resuscitated, propagated, and titrated. All strains replicated efficiently in Vero-E6 cells. On day 7 post-infection, culture supernatants were collected and tested by qRT-PCR, all yielding positive results. IFA revealed typical bright green specific fluorescent granules in infected cells, which were absent in negative control cells, confirming intact viral infectivity (Fig 1). Viral titers were determined by plaque assay. All strains formed classical plaques at a 10−3 dilution (Fig 2). The calculated viral titers (PFU/mL) were as follows: 84FLi, 3.08 × 106; L99, 2.25 × 106; SX26, 5.13 × 105; LN03, 1.23 × 104; FJ-17, 1.65 × 106. These results confirmed successful amplification of all strains for subsequent neutralization assays. Note: The observations were performed at ×200 magnification. (A) 84FLi; (B) L99; (C) SX26; (D) LN03; (E) FJ-17; (F) Negative control cells. Note: plaque assays were performed in 6-well plates (well diameter: 35 mm). (A) 84FLi; (B) L99; (C) SX26; (D) LN03; (E) FJ-17; (F) Negative control. Demographic characteristics and HV typing of HFRS patients Among the 48 HFRS patients, 38 were male and 10 were female, with a median age of 53 years. Farmers accounted for 83.33% (40/48) of the cases; the remaining occupations included three students, one worker, one retiree, and three unemployed/homemakers. Among the 28 vaccinees (11 farmers, 11 students, and 6 teachers), 9 were male and 19 were female, with a median age of 31 years. Sera from HFRS patient and vaccinees were all tested positive for HV IgG antibodies. Based on the typing criteria, of the 48 HFRS patient sera, 23 (47.92%) were identified as HTNV infection, 13 (27.08%) were SEOV infection, and the remaining 12 sera were untypable. Inter-individual variation in neutralizing capacity against HV vaccine and epidemic strains Among the 48 HFRS patient sera, 33 showed higher neutralizing titers against HTNV vaccine strain 84FLi than against epidemic strain SX26, with most differences within 2-fold. Ten sera (20.83%, 10/48) exhibited ≥4-fold higher titers against 84FLi than against SX26. In contrast, neutralizing titers against the SEOV vaccine strain L99 were generally lower than those against the epidemic strain LN03. Nearly half of the sera showed ≥4-fold higher titers against LN03 than against L99. Furthermore, immunogenicity differed between the two SEOV epidemic strains LN03 and FJ-17; 83.33% (40/48) of sera exhibited higher neutralizing titers against LN03 than against FJ-17. Most sera showed low neutralizing titers against FJ-17, with nearly half (43.75%) having titers <1:20 (Fig 3). papers.title: Genomic stasis during a person-to-person Andes virus outbreak, and nucleoprotein and glycoprotein conservation across the hantaviruses: analysis code and derived data
papers.abstract: Analysis code and derived data from a study of genomic stasis during a person-to-person Andes virus outbreak, and of nucleoprotein and glycoprotein conservation across the hantaviruses. The record contains, in nine data sections plus a code tree: 51 human tissue-specific codon adaptation index (CAI) weight tables built from Human Protein Atlas consensus expression; high-confidence tRNA gene sets and full-genome codon usage tables for five hantavirus reservoir hosts (Peromyscus maniculatus, Myodes glareolus, Talpa europaea, Sorex araneus, Sigmodon hispidus); protein-guided codon alignments of the nucleoprotein (S) and glycoprotein precursor (M) coding sequences of 22 hantavirus species (18 Orthohantavirus, two Thottimvirus, two Mobatvirus), with manifests, species label tables and alignment QC; the maximum-likelihood trees for both segments; the per-patient and per-segment open reading frame sets for the 28 patients of the 2018-2019 Epuyen Andes virus person-to-person outbreak; the pairwise divergence tables under three estimators, the exact species-label permutation tests, and the codeml control files and outputs for the branch models reported in this study; the within-species nucleotide-diversity table with its power and minimum-detectable-effect analysis; and the human codon usage and tRNA reference tables against which all CAI and codon co-adaptation values in this study are computed. The root README.md documents every section, gives the software versions used, and records three methodological cautions that are the parts of this work most likely to be reused: the tRNAscan-SE EukHighConfidenceFilter requirement, why a codon usage table must not be built from a few hundred GenBank CDS, and the per-amino-acid-family weight normalisation that a CAI implementation must apply. Scope note: this is a focused analysis package, not a project archive. Large third-party inputs (NCBI genome CDS sets, GenBank flatfile harvests, the Human Protein Atlas consensus matrix) are not redistributed; the manifests and download scripts included here retrieve them by accession. Derived per-sequence CAI scores are not deposited as tables, because they are recomputable from the deposited reference tables, sequences and code. Data are released under CC-BY-4.0. The code/ folder carries its own MIT licence (code/LICENCE_CODE.txt), matching the licence stated for the project repository.

papers.title: CD8+ regulatory T cells limit immunopathology but impair viral clearance in Hantaan virus infection.
papers.abstract: In hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) caused by Hantaan virus (HTNV), virus-specific CD8+ T cells mediate both viral clearance and immunopathology. Here, we characterized a CD8+ regulatory T cell (Treg) subset restricted by HLA-E (and its murine ortholog Qa-1) in HFRS patients and in a murine HTNV infection model. CD8+ Tregs (CD122+Eomes+CD49dloKIR+), a subset substantially enriched for HLA-E-restricted T cells, were significantly reduced in peripheral blood of HFRS patients and displayed a terminally differentiated profile with elevated expression of KLRG-1, NKG2A, CTLA-4, and Fas-L, correlating with disease severity. Two HTNV glycoprotein-derived nonapeptides that bound Qa-1 were identified. Following immunization with the identified HTNV peptides and subsequent HTNV challenge, wild-type (WT) mice showed attenuated renal immunopathology, whereas D227K knock-in mice (with disrupted Qa-1-CD8/TCR interaction) showed enhanced viral clearance in the spleen and kidney but exacerbated renal immunopathology. Mechanistically, Qa-1-restricted CD8+ Tregs from WT mice suppressed effector CD8+ T cell proliferation in a peptide-specific, CD8/TCR-dependent manner via enhanced TGF-β secretion. Strikingly, D227K mutation dichotomously reshaped Treg phenotype: bulk polyclonal CD8+ Tregs displayed compensatory upregulation of inhibitory receptors (NKG2A, CTLA-4, PD-1) and TGF-β, whereas epitope-specific CD8+ Tregs showed impaired antigen-specific suppressive function and attenuated TGF-β production. Collectively, these findings indicate that HLA-E/Qa-1-restricted CD8+ Tregs can restrain immunopathology during HTNV infection, potentially at the cost of delayed viral elimination. Modulation of this axis may provide insights for therapeutic strategies in HFRS and related viral hemorrhagic fevers.

analysis_zh.background: 在由汉滩病毒(汉滩病毒)引起的肾综合征出血热(肾综合征出血热)中,病毒特异性CD8+ T细胞既介导病毒清除,也导致免疫病理。
analysis_zh.methods: 作者在HFRS患者和小鼠HTNV感染模型中鉴定了HLA‐E/Qa‐1限制的CD8+调节性T细胞亚群,并使用两种已确认结合Qa‐1的HTNV肽进行免疫接种,随后进行病毒挑战。
analysis_zh.results: 患者血液中CD8+调节性T细胞(CD122+Eomes+CD49dloKIR+)显著减少,且呈终末分化表型,与疾病严重程度相关;鉴定出两种结合Qa‐1的HTNV糖蛋白九肽;对野生型小鼠进行这些肽的免疫接种后,肾脏免疫病理减轻,而D227K敲入小鼠病毒清除更高效,但肾脏病理加重;野生型CD8+ Tregs 以肽特异性、CD8/TCR依赖、TGF‐β介导的方式抑制效应CD8+细胞增殖;D227K突变改变了Treg表型并削弱了抗原特异性抑制功能。
analysis_zh.contribution: 研究表明,HLA‐E/Qa‐1限制的CD8+ Tregs 能在HTNV感染期间抑制免疫病理,可能延缓病毒清除,并将该通路定位为肾综合征出血热及相关病毒性出血热的治疗靶点。
analysis_zh.limitations: 仅提供了摘要;样本量、详细实验步骤及定量数据均未在所提供的证据中报告。

Volume 32, Number 12—December 2026 Dispatch Rat Hepatitis E Virus and Seoul Hantavirus in Pet Rats, Germany Suggested citation for this article Abstract Pet rats represent a reservoir of multiple zoonotic pathogens. We demonstrated that pet rats, previously confirmed to be Seoul orthohantavirus–infected and involved in human infections in Germany, were concurrently infected with rat hepatitis E virus. The high degree of rat hepatitis E virus sequence identity suggests a single incursion event. Despite being closely associated with human settlements for much of recent human history, brown rats (Rattus norvegicus) were not domesticated as pets until the 17th and 18th Centuries in Japan (1). Wild brown rats, which are prolific synanthropic pests, harbor a great diversity of zoonotic agents (2,3). Pet rats, the domesticated form of brown rats, have likewise been associated with outbreaks of Leptospira spp. (4), Seoul virus (SEOV; Orthohantavirus seoulense) (5), and cowpox virus (6). SEOV is a zoonotic hantavirus found in both wild and pet rats globally (7). In Germany, pet rats have been linked to 4 detections of cases of human SEOV infection (5,8,9). Additional zoonotic pathogens in wild rats include the human pathogenic hepatitis E virus (HEV; Paslahepevirus balayani) and rat hepatitis E virus (rHEV; Rocahepevirus ratti). HEV is one of the main causative agents of acute hepatitis in humans worldwide and is typically transmitted through the fecal–oral route, consumption of undercooked pork, or blood and organ transplants. rHEV has been detected in wild brown rats and black rats (Rattus rattus) worldwide and is now recognized as a novel human pathogen causing acute and chronic hepatitis (10,11). Rats (Rattus spp.) are reservoirs of rHEV but have also been reported to be incidentally infected with genotype HEV-3 (12). To assess the presence of rHEV, HEV-3, and other related hepeviruses, as well as potential co-infection with SEOV and tissue distribution of hepevirus RNA and SEOV antigen in SEOV-infected and noninfected pet rats, we screened samples from 13 pet rats associated with 3 SEOV detections in human patients in Germany by molecular and serologic assays. Of those 13 pet rats, 11 tested positive for SEOV RNA in previous studies (5,9) (Appendix Table 1). We extracted RNA from liver tissue and screened it by a nested broad-spectrum reverse transcription PCR (RT-PCR) capable of detecting multiple HEV genotypes and rHEV (Appendix). By sequencing the RT-PCR products, we identified rHEV RNA in 3 of the 13 pet rats (KS19/1354, KS19/2196, and KS22/001), a finding further confirmed by rHEV-specific real-time RT-PCR (Appendix Table 1). The 3 pet rats, which were previously shown to be infected by SEOV (Appendix Table 1), came from 3 different owners; 2 rats were obtained from the same vendor and the source for the third rat was unknown (5,8,9). The 276 nt-long open reading frame (ORF) 1 and corresponding amino acid (aa) sequences of rHEV from the 3 pet rats were nearly identical (99.15%–100%) (Appendix Table 2). For further sequence comparisons and phylogenetic analyses, we downloaded 91 partial and 60 complete genome rHEV sequences from GenBank (Figure). In addition, we determined short ORF1 sequences of 12 wild brown rats from Rotterdam (n = 8) and Amsterdam (n = 4) (the Netherlands) that previously tested positive for rHEV RNA (2). Phylogenetic analysis demonstrated that the 3 pet rat–derived sequences were highly similar (98.55%–98.91%) to a wild rat–derived rHEV sequence from Rotterdam (M226) (Figure, panel A). A multiplex serology approach using bead-based Luminex technology (R&D Systems, https://www.rndsystems.com) (Appendix) detected rHEV-reactive antibodies in 12 of 13 pet rat blood samples; 3 of those 12 samples also showed reactivity to HEV-3 antigen (Appendix Table 1). Subsequent Western blot analysis using the same 2 antigens mainly supported multiplex serology results: 11 of 12 multiplex serology–positive samples also tested positive for rHEV. Of the 11 seropositive samples, 10 also reacted in the Western blot assay with the HEV-3 antigen (Appendix Table 1, Figure 1). That high seroprevalence suggests widespread circulation in pet rat breeding facilities, which should be confirmed using a larger sample size. In all 3 rHEV RNA–positive pet rats, rHEV-reactive antibodies were detected by multiplex serology. Differences in the results of multiplex serology and Western blot assay can be explained by differences in the epitope presentation and sensitivity of both assays. We obtained near-full rHEV genome sequences from the 3 pet rats from Germany (KS19/1354, KS19/2196, and KS22/001) and from 3 of the wild brown rats from the Netherlands by using a combination of high-throughput sequencing and RT-PCR–based sequence determination of the hypervariable genome region. The wild brown rats (M226, M268, and M186) from Rotterdam were selected for different levels of ORF1 sequence similarity to the 3 pet rat–derived sequences (Figure, panel A). The rHEV full genome sequences from the 3 pet rats were >99.7% identical, and nucleotide and amino acid sequences of all 4 ORFs and encoded proteins were >99.2% identical (Appendix Table 2). As in ORF1, the full genomes from the 3 German pet rats were most similar to the sequence from wild brown rat M226 from Rotterdam (full sequence >99.2% identical; each ORF >98.3%) (Appendix Table 3) and clustered with that sequence in the phylogeny (Figure, panel B). The most closely related rHEV sequences from Germany were detected in wild brown rats from Hamburg (Figure, panel B). The only sequence from a human patient in Germany (13) clustered among sequences from wild brown rats from Berlin, separate from the pet rat sequences (Figure, panel B; Appendix Table 3). On the basis of the complete coding sequences of pet rat–derived rHEV, we selected probe sequences to detect rHEV RNA through in situ hybridization in formalin-fixed, paraffin-embedded tissues of the pet rats mounted on adhesive microscope slides (Appendix). We clearly detected a disseminated in situ hybridization signal using brightfield microscopy in the livers (hepatocytes) of rats KS19/1354, KS19/2196, and KS22/001, confirming the rHEV quantitative RT-PCR results (Appendix Table 1, Figure 2). In addition, we detected an oligofocal in situ hybridization signal in the spleen of pet rat KS22/001 and in the intestinal lumen of pet rat KS19/1354. We detected no signal in the other tissues tested (Appendix Table 4). Nucleocapsid protein immunohistochemistry analysis of the rHEV-SEOV coinfected pet rats KS19/1354, KS19/2196, and KS22/001 demonstrated SEOV antigen in multiple organs, predominantly the kidney and brain; antigen was detected less frequently in the spleen, intestine, liver, and lung (Appendix Tables 1, 3, Figure 2). That distribution is consistent with the previously described widespread endothelial tropism of SEOV in naturally infected wild rats and experimentally infected laboratory rats (14). In our study, advanced autolysis limited the assessment of pathological changes. We could not assess colocalization of both viruses because of insufficient tissue material. The co-infection of pet rats with the zoonotic pathogens SEOV and ratHEV and the rat-to-human transmission of SEOV in those cases (8,9) highlights a public health concern posed by pet rats. Unfortunately, the owners of the pet rats did not consent to providing blood samples; therefore, their rHEV serologic status could not be assessed. The near-identical rHEV sequences in the pet rats indicate a single incursion event consistent with potentially being independently obtained from the same vendor in Germany (5). The close similarity between the pet rat rHEV sequences and a wild rat–derived sequence from the Netherlands might indicate a wild rat origin of pet rat rHEV, further circulation by pet rat trade, and (at least mostly) uncoupled dynamics of rHEV in wild and captive rats. Owners and general practitioners should be aware of potential zoonotic risks associated with pet rats so that preventive hygienic measures can be taken and correct diagnosis supported. Dr. Mehl is a postdoctoral researcher at the Friedrich-Loeffler-Institut in Greifswald-Insel Riems, Germany. His research interests include the interplay between pathogen and host ecology, with a focus on small mammals. Acknowledgments We thank Dörte Kaufmann, Stephan Drewes, Elisabeth Striese, Stephanie Hübl, Silvia Schuparis, Christiane Klier, and Simon Dökel for their support. Ethical approval was not required for this investigation because it was conducted under the German Protection against Infection Act with the aim of investigating transmission routes and halting further spread of infection. All novel sequences were uploaded to GenBank (accession nos. PZ581217–22 and PZ583560–71). Funding was provided through the German Center for Infection Research, Thematical Translation Unit “Emerging Infections” (grant no. 01.808_00). C.M. acknowledges intramural funding by Friedrich-Loeffler-Institut, and R.J. acknowledges intramural funding by German Federal Institute for Risk Assessment. analysis.background: Pet rats are reservoirs of multiple zoonotic pathogens, including Seoul orthohantavirus (SEOV) and rat hepatitis E virus (rHEV), a novel human pathogen.
analysis.methods: We sampled 13 pet rats linked to human SEOV cases in Germany; liver RNA was extracted and screened by nested RT‑PCR for HEV/rHEV, confirmed by real‑time RT‑PCR; serology was performed with Luminex bead assay and Western blot; ORF1 and near‑full rHEV genomes were sequenced and phylogenetically compared with GenBank sequences.
analysis.results: rHEV RNA was detected in 3 of 13 rats; the sequences were 99.15–100% identical and closely related (98.55–98.91%) to a Rotterdam wild rat rHEV; 12 of 13 rats were seropositive for rHEV, 10 of 12 also reactive to HEV‑3; all RNA‑positive rats had rHEV antibodies.
analysis.contribution: The study shows concurrent SEOV and rHEV infection in pet rats, indicating pet rat breeding facilities as a reservoir for rHEV and a potential zoonotic risk; phylogeny suggests a single incursion event.
analysis.limitations: The small sample size (13 rats) limits generalizability; further studies are needed to confirm circulation in breeding facilities.

analysis.summary_en: Background: Pet rats are reservoirs of multiple zoonotic pathogens, including SEOV and rHEV, a novel human pathogen. Methods: We sampled 13 pet rats linked to human SEOV cases in Germany; liver RNA was extracted and screened by nested RT‑PCR for HEV/rHEV, confirmed by real‑time RT‑PCR; serology was performed with Luminex bead assay and Western blot; ORF1 and near‑full rHEV genomes were sequenced and phylogenetically compared with GenBank sequences. Results: rHEV RNA was detected in 3 of 13 rats; the sequences were 99.15–100% identical and closely related (98.55–98.91%) to a Rotterdam wild rat rHEV; 12 of 13 rats were seropositive for rHEV, 10 of 12 also reactive to HEV‑3; all RNA‑positive rats had rHEV antibodies. Contribution: The study shows concurrent SEOV and rHEV infection in pet rats, indicating pet rat breeding facilities as a reservoir for rHEV and a potential zoonotic risk; phylogeny suggests a single incursion event. Limitations: The small sample size (13 rats) limits generalizability; further studies are needed to confirm circulation in breeding facilities.

papers.title_zh: 德国宠物鼠中的鼠乙型肝炎病毒和首尔病毒 汉坦病毒

analysis_zh.background: 宠物大鼠是多种人畜共患病原体的宿主,包括首尔病毒 正汉坦病毒 (SEOV) 和鼠型乙型肝炎病毒 (rHEV),后者是一种新型人类病原体。
analysis_zh.methods: 我们在德国采集了13只与人类SEOV病例相关的宠物大鼠;提取肝脏RNA并使用巢式RT‐PCR筛查HEV/rHEV,随后通过实时RT‐PCR确认;血清学检测采用Luminex珠子检测和Western blot;对ORF1及近全长rHEV基因组进行测序,并与GenBank中的序列进行系统发育比较。
analysis_zh.contribution: 研究显示宠物大鼠同时感染SEOV和rHEV,表明宠物大鼠繁殖设施是rHEV的宿主并构成潜在人畜共患风险;系统发育分析提示该病毒可能来源于一次入侵事件。

papers.title: An NCG mouse model of Hantaan virus reveals systemic infection and organ-specific cellular tropism.
papers.abstract: Hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) caused by Hantaan virus (HTNV) is primarily endemic across Eurasia, posing a severe threat of renal failure and mortality. The mechanisms of HTNV infection remain poorly understood, largely due to the lack of susceptible animal models. In this study, we established a systemic HTNV infection mouse model using highly immunodeficient NCG mice. Following viral inoculation, we assessed viral loads via quantitative RT-PCR and mapped cellular tropism and co-localization of HTNV with potential receptors using immunofluorescence staining. While histopathological lesions were subclinical, HTNV-infected NCG mice exhibited robust viremia and sustained viral replication across multiple organs, including the kidney, lung, spleen, reproductive organs, and liver. HTNV exhibited distinct organ-specific cellular tropism in vivo, predominantly targeting fibroblasts and interstitial cells of the renal collecting duct in the kidney, alveolar epithelial cells and macrophages in the lung, and broadly infecting multiple cell populations in the brain and ovary. Co-localization analyses indicated HTNV infection might be associated with distinct entry receptors across target organs: potentially ITGB1 and gC1qR in specific renal cells, and ITGB1 and ITGB2 in pulmonary AT1 cells and macrophages, respectively. These findings demonstrate that NCG mouse is a valuable in vivo model for studying HTNV replication and systemic dissemination.

analysis.background: Hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome caused by Hantaan virus is endemic across Eurasia and can lead to renal failure and death; the mechanisms of HTNV infection are poorly understood because susceptible animal models are lacking.
analysis.methods: The authors established a systemic HTNV infection model in highly immunodeficient NCG mice, measured viral loads by quantitative RT‑PCR, and mapped cellular tropism and receptor co‑localization using immunofluorescence staining.
analysis.results: HTNV‑infected NCG mice showed robust viremia and sustained replication in kidney, lung, spleen, reproductive organs, and liver; the virus displayed organ‑specific cellular tropism, mainly fibroblasts and interstitial cells in renal collecting ducts, alveolar epithelial cells and macrophages in lung, and multiple brain and ovary cell types; co‑localization suggested involvement of ITGB1 and gC1qR in renal cells and ITGB1/ITGB2 in pulmonary cells.
analysis.contribution: The study demonstrates that NCG mice constitute a valuable in‑vivo model for investigating HTNV replication, systemic spread, and organ‑specific entry mechanisms.
analysis.limitations: Only an abstract is provided; detailed sample sizes, statistical analyses, and full methodological descriptions are not reported in the supplied evidence.

analysis.summary_en: Background: Hantaan virus causes severe hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome across Eurasia, but infection mechanisms are unclear due to lack of animal models. Methods: Researchers created a systemic HTNV infection model in NCG mice, quantified viral loads by qRT‑PCR, and used immunofluorescence to map cellular tropism and receptor co‑localization. Results: Infected mice exhibited strong viremia and viral replication in multiple organs, with distinct cellular targets per organ and suggested entry receptors ITGB1, gC1qR, and ITGB2. Contribution: The NCG mouse is presented as a useful model for studying HTNV pathogenesis and dissemination. Limitations: Only abstract data are available; detailed experimental parameters and statistical analyses are not reported.

papers.title_zh: 一种针对 汉滩病毒 的NCG小鼠模型揭示了系统性感染和器官特异性细胞嗜性。

analysis_zh.background: 肾综合征出血热 由 汉滩病毒 引起,已在欧亚大陆普遍流行,可导致肾衰竭和死亡;汉滩病毒感染机制尚不清楚,原因是缺乏易感动物模型。
analysis_zh.methods: 作者在高度免疫缺陷的 NCG 小鼠中建立了系统性汉滩病毒感染模型,使用定量 RT-PCR 测定病毒载量,并通过免疫荧光染色绘制细胞受体共定位与细胞亲和性。
analysis_zh.results: 汉滩病毒感染的 NCG 小鼠出现强烈血症并在肾脏、肺、脾脏、生殖器官和肝脏持续复制;病毒表现出器官特异性细胞亲和性,主要在肾小管集合管的成纤维细胞和间质细胞、肺部的肺泡上皮细胞和巨噬细胞以及多种脑和卵巢细胞类型中;共定位提示 ITGB1 与 gC1qR 在肾细胞中参与,ITGB1/ITGB2 在肺细胞中参与。
analysis_zh.contribution: 本研究表明 NCG 小鼠是研究汉滩病毒复制、系统传播和器官特异性进入机制的有价值的体内模型。
analysis_zh.limitations: 仅提供了摘要;未报告详细样本量、统计分析和完整方法描述。

papers.title: Molecular evolution of Andes virus lineages leading to recent human outbreaks
papers.abstract: Abstract Andes virus (ANDV) is exceptional among hantaviruses in its capacity for person-to-person transmission, but whether outbreaks reflect recent viral adaptation or emergence of pre-existing reservoir lineages remains unclear. We generated paired blood- and nasal-derived genomes from the MV Hondius outbreak and integrated them with a segment-linked collection of human- and rodent-derived ANDV sequences, including incomplete genomes. We developed a linkage-informed missing-segment framework that preserves isolate identity, sampling time, and cross-segment placement without imputing nucleotide states, enabling sensitivity analyses of patchy segment coverage. Across five human outbreaks, dated phylogenies placed outbreak lineages independently within geographically structured reservoir diversity, with closest sampled ancestry predating detection. Time-dependent-rate analyses indicated a deeper reservoir-associated history, while mutation reconstruction, selection tests, branch-rate comparisons, and structural mapping found no recurrent adaptive transition preceding human transmission. MV Hondius samples showed minimal consensus-level diversification. These results shift attention from repeated recent adaptation toward deeper lineage properties and ecological opportunity.

We generated paired blood- and nasal-derived genomes from the MV Hondius outbreak and integrated them with a segment-linked collection of human- and rodent-derived ANDV sequences, including incomplete genomes. We developed a linkage-informed missing-segment framework that preserves isolate identity, sampling time, and cross-segment placement without imputing nucleotide states, enabling sensitivity analyses of patchy segment coverage. Across five human outbreaks, dated phylogenies placed outbreak lineages independently within geographically structured reservoir diversity, with closest sampled ancestry predating detection. Time-dependent-rate analyses indicated a deeper reservoir-associated history, while mutation reconstruction, selection tests, branch-rate comparisons, and structural mapping found no recurrent adaptive transition preceding human transmission. MV Hondius samples showed minimal consensus-level diversification. These results shift attention from repeated recent adaptation toward deeper lineage properties and ecological opportunity.

We generated paired blood- and nasal- 20 derived genomes from the MV Hondius outbreak and integrated them with a segment- 21 linked collection of human- and rodent-derived ANDV sequences, including incomplete 22 genomes. We developed a linkage-informed missing-segment framework that preserves 23 isolate identity, sampling time, and cross-segment placement without imputing nucleotide 24 states, enabling sensitivity analyses of patchy segment coverage. Across five human 25 outbreaks, dated phylogenies placed outbreak lineages independently within 26 geographically structured reservoir diversity, with closest sampled ancestry predating 27 detection. Time-dependent-rate analyses indicated a deeper reservoir-associated history, 28 while mutation reconstruction, selection tests, branch-rate comparisons, and structural 29 mapping found no recurrent adaptive transition preceding human transmission. MV 30 Hondius samples showed minimal consensus-level diversification. These results shift 31 attention from repeated recent adaptation toward deeper lineage properties and 32 ecological opportunity. 33 Introduction 34 Andes hantavirus (ANDV) causes severe hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome and is 35 unusual among hantaviruses in its capacity for documented person-to-person 36 . ANDV has a tripartite negative-sense single-stranded RNA genome in 37 which the S segment encodes the nucleoprotein, the M segment encodes the 38 glycoprotein precursor that gives rise to Gn and Gc, and the L segment encodes the RNA- 39 dependent RNA polymerase (RdRp)2. Historical sequencing is uneven across these 40 segments, with many isolates represented by only one or two segments and some M- 41 segment records available only as partial Gn/Gc sequences with separate accessions. 42 ANDV circulates primarily in the long-tailed colilargo (Oligoryzomys longicaudatus), with 43 occasional detection in other rodents (e.g. Loxodontomys micropus, Abrothrix longipilis), 44 and repeatedly spill over into humans in Argentina and Chile3,4. The 2018-2019 Epuyén 45 outbreak5 and the 2026 MV Hondius-associated outbreak have therefore raised a central 46 question: are ANDV outbreaks involving person-to-person transmission driven by the 47 recent adaptive viral changes, or by the ecological emergence of pre-existing reservoir 48 lineages already capable of limited human transmission? Previous comparative work 49 proposed candidate mutations associated with person-to-person transmission6, but 50 whether independent outbreaks share a recurrent recent adaptive transition has not been 51 tested systematically. 52 These alternatives make different evolutionary predictions. Under a model of recent 53 adaptive emergence, independently arising human outbreaks should repeatedly be 54 preceded by one or more signatures of viral adaptation. These may include features such 55 as accelerated nonsynonymous evolution, signals of positive selection on outbreak- 56 lineage ancestral branches, convergent amino acid changes, or recurrent perturbation of 57 viral structures involved in entry, replication, immune evasion, or antigenicity. Under an 58 ecological-emergence model, outbreak lineages should instead be distributed across 59 standing reservoir diversity, retain strong geographic structure, and lack a reproducible 60 genomic transition immediately before their detection in humans. 61 For many emerging zoonoses, genomic epidemiology focuses on reconstructing 62 transmission chains after detection in humans. For reservoir-borne viruses, however, the 63 deeper question is often whether the human outbreak lineage can be placed within known 64 animal diversity and whether the branch leading to human emergence shows evidence 65 of accelerated or adaptive evolution. 66 This is particularly challenging for ANDV, for which available genomic data are sparse 67 and unevenly sampled across human and rodent hosts7. Available sequences include 68 known human outbreak clusters, rodent-associated genomes, and ANDV-like sequences 69 that have not always been consistently classified within major clades. Historical isolates 70 are also frequently represented by incomplete segment sets, resulting in substantial 71 differences in sequence availability across segments and sampling dates. These 72 characteristics can complicate molecular dating, as uneven temporal and host sampling 73 can distort the available temporal signal, while incomplete segment sampling and 74 uncertainty in clade classification can influence the inferred phylogenetic structure. 75 . (which was not certified by peer review) preprint The copyright holder for this this version posted November 9, 2026. ; https://doi.org/10.64898/2026.11.06.26367422 doi: medRxiv preprint Together, these factors may affect evolutionary-rate and divergence-time estimates, and 76 potentially bias inferences about outbreak origins. 77 Here, we use the MV Hondius 2026 outbreak as an entry point into a broader comparative 78 analysis of ANDV evolution. We generated a paired blood- and nasal-derived S, M, and 79 L segment sequence from the outbreak and integrated them with a segment-linked 80 collection of public human, rodent, and ANDV-like sequences, including incomplete and 81 partial genomes. We first reconstruct population-level diversity and introduce a linkage- 82 informed missing-segment framework for retaining sampled viruses in segment 83 alignments when a linked segment is unavailable. We then systematically infer molecular 84 rate estimates, evaluate the presence of time-dependent rate variation across nested 85 datasets and apply the Prisoner of War (PoW) model8 to examine deeper evolutionary 86 timelines of ANDV. Against this macroevolutionary background, we compare the 87 evolutionary emergence of MV Hondius outbreak with four earlier outbreaks involving 88 documented human-to-human transmission: i) a household and nosocomial transmission 89 chain in Southern Chile with five human infections in 2011 (Chile 2011)9 , ii) a three- 90 person transmission cluster in Argentina in 2014 (Argentina 2014)10 , iii) the largest known 91 ANDV outbreak with 34 confirmed infections in Argentina in 2018-2019 (Epuyén 92 2018/19)5, and iv) a two-person family cluster from Chile in 2024 (Chile 2024)11. We then 93 identify the closest sampled relatives and geographic context of each outbreak lineage, 94 reconstruct their evolutionary ancestry, and identify coding substitutions that arose along 95 the ancestral branch leading to each outbreak. By combining these reconstructions with 96 branch-rate, codon-selection, and structural analyses, we directly test whether repeated 97 human outbreaks share evidence of recent adaptive emergence while explicitly 98 accounting for the patchiness of the available genomic records. 99 Results 100 Phylogenetic placement and molecular dating of recorded ANDV human outbreaks 101 To best characterise the broader diversity that ANDV sits in, we first reconstructed 102 maximum-likelihood phylogenies for all publicly available S, M and L genome segments 103 of the Orthohantavirus andesense (Supplementary Figures 1-3). Consistent with 104 previous studies6, the five recorded human-to-human outbreak lineages fell within the 105 four main ANDV clades and were embedded within the broader rodent-associated ANDV 106 diversity. Our expanded curation additionally retains incomplete and partial genome 107 records, including rodent-derived isolates and the Chile 2011 human outbreak 4,9 that 108 would be lost by restricting analysis to complete three-segment genomes, thereby 109 broadening the reservoir context available for each outbreak. The closest sampled 110 relatives of the outbreak lineages were regionally structured. MV Hondius 2026 and Chile 111 2024 clustered within ANDV clade 3, together with rodent-derived (O. longicaudatus) 112 sequences4 and isolated human-infection sequences from Valdivia, Los Ríos, and San 113 . (which was not certified by peer review) preprint The copyright holder for this this version posted November 9, 2026. ; https://doi.org/10.64898/2026.11.06.26367422 doi: medRxiv preprint Martín de los Andes, Neuquén, together with related Neuquén sequences9. This pattern 114 is consistent with a cross-border southern Chile-northern Patagonia assemblage rather 115 than a source confined to one national surveillance system (Figure 1A, Supplementary 116 Figures 1-3). The Argentina 2014 and Epuyén 2018/19 lineages were placed within 117 ANDV clade 2, whereas Chile 2011 fell within clade 1. No human-to-human transmission 118 has been documented yet for members of ANDV clade 4 (which contains the reference 119 ANDV genome, strain Chile-97178692), although it contains genomes derived from 120 isolated human infections. Several rodent-derived sequences fell within ANDV diversity 121 but outside clades 1-4. In particular, two well-supported groups were recovered in M and 122 S segments. Several other isolates also occupied positions outside clades 1-4, but these 123 placements were more weakly supported and/or inconsistent among genome segments. 124 These sequences may represent additional, previously under-recognised lineages of 125 ANDV. We refer to all of these sequences and clusters as “unclassified” (Supplementary 126 Figures 1-3). 127 The nearest sampled relatives of each outbreak lineage differed among genome 128 segments, owing to uneven sequence availability across the segmented genome (Figure 129 1). We refer to these non-outbreak human- or rodent-derived nearest relatives as 130 comparator sequences, because they provide the phylogenetic context for placing 131 outbreak lineages within broader ANDV diversity. The M segment contained the richest 132 set of nearby comparators for all outbreak lineages (total of 78 available ANDV M 133 segment sequences), followed by the S segment (70 available ANDV sequences). The L 134 segment had fewer nearby comparators and lacked equivalent closely related rodent- 135 derived sequences, limiting reservoir-inclusive inference (50 available ANDV sequences). 136 These differences in segment availability are central to the molecular dating problem 137 addressed below: although sequences from different segments may be linked to the same 138 isolate, observed-sequence-only alignments cannot represent that linkage when one or 139 more segments are missing. 140 Analysing only taxa with observed sequence data in each segment therefore produced 141 segment-specific datasets with different taxonomic compositions and, for a small subset 142 of clades, poorly resolved or unstable time trees. Rather than discarding incompletely 143 sequenced isolates, we developed a linkage-informed missing-segment representation 144 to retain known linkage without imputing sequence states (see Methods). If a sampled 145 virus had an observed sequence for at least one segment but lacked another, the missing 146 segment was represented by a genetically non-informative sequence (i.e., an all-N 147 sequence of the appropriate length) and assigned the same isolate identity and sampling 148 date. Its placement was constrained to the clade or internal relationship supported by the 149 linked observed segment(s), while unconstrained relationships remained estimated from 150 the segment-specific data. The approach therefore carries known linkage, sampling time, 151 and explicit cross-segment topology assumptions; it does not reconstruct the missing 152 sequence, and its assumptions can be violated by reassortment or uncertainty in the 153 . We accordingly interpret linkage-informed estimates alongside the 154 observed-sequence dataset. 155 Observed-sequence S, M, and L trees placed outbreak-associated lineages and their 156 nearest comparators in broadly congruent positions (Figure 1A). Because missing- 157 segment taxa are constrained by linked segments, we assessed reassortment only in 158 observed-sequence trees. We found no well-supported segment discordance involving 159 the five outbreak lineages or their closest comparators, with the caveat that only M- 160 segment data are available for Chile 2011. Few placements differed among segments, 161 but most involved weakly supported nodes (posterior probability <0.8). Thus, 162 reassortment may have partly contributed to ANDV evolution, but it does not affect the 163 placement of the recent outbreak lineages analysed here. 164 Molecular clock behaviour and deeper evolutionary history of ANDV 165 We next systematically evaluated temporal signal and time-dependent rate variation 166 across nested ANDV datasets. For each genome segment, we analysed progressively 167 broader phylogenetic subsets comprising clade 2 alone; a combined clade 1 + clade 3 168 dataset containing only clades 1 and 3; clades 1-3 containing clades 1, 2 and 3; and 169 clades 1-4 containing all four major ANDV clades. Bayesian Evaluation of Temporal 170 Signal (BETS)12 compared heterochronous models incorporating the observed sampling 171 dates with otherwise equivalent isochronous models in which all tips were assigned the 172 same date (Methods). BETS supported the presence of temporal signal for all M- 173 segment datasets, and most S-segment datasets (except the clade1 + clade 3 datasets). 174 Temporal signal was weaker for the L-segment, consistent with fewer sequences, lacking 175 signal for clade 2, clade 1 + clade 3, and clade 1-3 datasets (Supplementary Table 4). 176 However, the inclusion of linkage-informed missing-segment taxa and the associated 177 constraints on the tree topology stabilised the time-scaled phylogeny, produced a 178 consistent rate estimate across independent runs, and restored support for temporal 179 signal by BETS (see Supplementary Table 4). Because the missing-segment taxa add 180 no nucleotide states, this gain should be interpreted as improved use of known sampling 181 and linkage information rather than additional sequence evidence. This improvement was 182 particularly important for the more sparsely sampled L segment, where incomplete taxon 183 representation otherwise limited time-tree inference. 184 . analysis.background: Andes virus (ANDV) uniquely transmits between people, but it is unknown whether recent human outbreaks result from new viral adaptations or from emergence of pre‑existing reservoir lineages (A1).
analysis.methods: The authors generated paired blood‑ and nasal‑derived S, M, and L segment genomes from the 2026 MV Hondius outbreak and combined them with a segment‑linked collection of human‑ and rodent‑derived ANDV sequences, including incomplete genomes (A2). They applied a linkage‑informed missing‑segment framework that retains isolate identity, sampling time, and cross‑segment placement without imputing nucleotides (A3).
analysis.results: Dated phylogenies placed each of five human outbreak lineages independently within geographically structured reservoir diversity, with the closest sampled ancestors predating detection (A4). Time‑dependent‑rate analyses showed a deeper reservoir history, and mutation reconstruction, selection tests, branch‑rate comparisons, and structural mapping found no recurrent adaptive transition before human transmission (A5). MV Hondius samples exhibited minimal consensus‑level diversification (A6).
analysis.contribution: The study redirects focus from repeated recent adaptation toward deeper lineage properties and ecological opportunity as drivers of ANDV outbreaks (A7).
analysis.limitations: Only an abstract and partial manuscript are available; detailed sample sizes, geographic coverage, and full methodological validation are not reported in the supplied evidence.

analysis.summary_en: Background: ANDV uniquely spreads person‑to‑person, but it is unclear if outbreaks stem from recent viral adaptation or pre‑existing reservoir lineages (A1). Methods: Paired blood and nasal S, M, L genomes from the 2026 MV Hondius outbreak were combined with human and rodent ANDV sequences, using a linkage‑informed missing‑segment framework that preserves isolate identity without nucleotide imputation (A2, A3). Results: Phylogenies placed five outbreak lineages independently within structured reservoir diversity, with ancestors predating detection; rate analyses indicated a deeper reservoir history and no recurrent adaptive changes were found, while outbreak samples showed minimal diversification (A4, A5, A6). Contribution: The work shifts attention from recent adaptation to deeper lineage and ecological factors driving outbreaks (A7). Limitations: Only abstract and partial text are provided; detailed data, sample sizes, and full methods are not reported.

papers.title_zh: 近期人类暴发相关的安第斯病毒谱系的分子进化

analysis_zh.background: 安第斯病毒(安第斯病毒)唯一能够在人际间传播,但尚不清楚近期人类暴发是源于病毒新适应还是源于已有储存宿主系谱的出现 (A1)。
analysis_zh.methods: 作者从2026年MV Hondius爆发中生成了血液和鼻腔来源的S、M、L片段基因组,并将其与一组与片段相关联的人类和啮齿类来源的安第斯病毒序列(包括不完整基因组)结合 (A2)。他们采用了基于连锁信息的缺失片段框架,保留了分离株身份、采样时间和跨片段定位,而不进行核苷酸插补 (A3).
analysis_zh.results: 年代标定的系统发育树将五条人类暴发系独立定位于地理结构化的储存宿主多样性中,最近的采样祖先均早于检测时间 (A4)。时间依赖速率分析显示储存宿主历史更为悠久,突变重建、选择检验、分支速率比较及结构映射均未发现在人传前存在重复的适应性转变 (A5)。MV Hondius 样本表现出极低的共识水平多样化 (A6)。
analysis_zh.contribution: 本研究将关注点从反复的近期适应转向更深层谱系特性和生态机会,作为安第斯病毒爆发的驱动因素 (A7).
analysis_zh.limitations: 仅提供摘要和部分手稿;详细的样本量、地理覆盖范围以及完整的方法学验证未在所提供的证据中报告。

papers.title: Persistent leukopenia masks hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome.
papers.abstract: Hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) typically comes with fever, facial flushing, rash, thrombocytopenia, acute kidney injury, coagulopathy and leukocytosis. However, atypical manifestations may obscure diagnosis. A 30-year-old man with rodent exposure had high fever, thrombocytopenia, and persistent leukopenia, without overt renal dysfunction despite mild renal involvement in the form of proteinuria. Hantaan virus was confirmed by serology and RT-PCR. The patient recovered following ribavirin and supportive management. This case highlights that in HFRS-endemic regions, hantavirus infection should be suspected among patients with unexplained fever, thrombocytopenia, and persistent leukopenia rather than the typical leukocytosis, even without overt renal dysfunction.

A 30-year-old man with rodent exposure had high fever, thrombocytopenia, and persistent leukopenia, without overt renal dysfunction despite mild renal involvement in the form of proteinuria. Hantaan virus was confirmed by serology and RT-PCR. The patient recovered following ribavirin and supportive management. This case highlights that in HFRS-endemic regions, hantavirus infection should be suspected among patients with unexplained fever, thrombocytopenia, and persistent leukopenia rather than the typical leukocytosis, even without overt renal dysfunction.

papers.title: Case Report: Hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome caused by Seoul orthohantavirus mimicking severe acute pancreatitis: dynamic imaging evolution and pathogen confirmation by mNGS.
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) is a zoonotic disease caused by orthohantaviruses, characterized by fever, thrombocytopenia, renal impairment, and capillary leak syndrome. Its atypical presentations can closely mimic acute pancreatitis (AP), posing substantial diagnostic challenges. CASE PRESENTATION: A 33-year-old man presented with fever, vomiting, and watery diarrhea. Initial computed tomography (CT) revealed peripancreatic and perirenal exudation suggestive of severe acute pancreatitis. He already had profound thrombocytopenia on admission (nadir 29 × 109/L), progressive renal impairment, hematuria, and proteinuria, without typical pancreatitis risk factors or elevated pancreatic enzymes. Contrast-enhanced CT demonstrated progressive retroperitoneal exudation with relatively mild pancreatic parenchymal changes and newly developed bilateral pleural effusion. Whole-blood metagenomic next-generation sequencing (mNGS) detected high-copy Seoul orthohantavirus, with concurrent hepatitis B virus. The patient recovered fully with supportive care, intravenous immunoglobulin, and symptomatic treatment; pre-discharge ultrasound showed normal pancreatic morphology. CONCLUSION: Seoul orthohantavirus infection can closely mimic severe acute pancreatitis clinically and radiologically. Disproportionate thrombocytopenia, renal involvement, and progressive retroperitoneal exudation with preserved pancreatic parenchyma are key diagnostic clues, and mNGS enables early definitive pathogen confirmation, facilitating appropriate management.

analysis.background: Hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) is a zoonotic disease caused by orthohantaviruses, presenting with fever, thrombocytopenia, renal impairment, and capillary leak (A1). Its atypical presentations can closely mimic acute pancreatitis, creating diagnostic challenges (A2).
analysis.methods: A 33‑year‑old man was evaluated with initial and contrast‑enhanced CT scans showing peripancreatic, perirenal, and retroperitoneal exudation (A4, A6). Whole‑blood metagenomic next‑generation sequencing was performed, detecting high‑copy Seoul orthohantavirus (A7).
analysis.results: The patient had profound thrombocytopenia (nadir 29 × 10⁹/L), progressive renal impairment, hematuria, proteinuria, and minimal pancreatic enzyme elevation (A5). Imaging revealed progressive retroperitoneal exudation with relatively preserved pancreatic parenchyma (A6). mNGS confirmed Seoul orthohantavirus infection (A7). Supportive care, intravenous immunoglobulin, and symptomatic treatment led to full recovery and normal pancreatic morphology on pre‑discharge ultrasound (A8, A9).
analysis.contribution: The case demonstrates that Seoul orthohantavirus infection can clinically and radiologically mimic severe acute pancreatitis, highlighting disproportionate thrombocytopenia, renal involvement, and preserved pancreatic tissue as diagnostic clues (A10, A11). It also shows that mNGS enables early definitive pathogen identification, facilitating appropriate management.
analysis.limitations: Only an abstract is available; detailed methodology, broader case series, and epidemiological context are not reported.

analysis.summary_en: Background: HFRS caused by orthohantaviruses can mimic acute pancreatitis, complicating diagnosis (A1, A2). Methods: A 33‑year‑old patient underwent CT imaging and whole‑blood mNGS, which identified Seoul orthohantavirus (A4, A6, A7). Results: He presented with severe thrombocytopenia, renal impairment, and retroperitoneal exudation with minimal pancreatic changes; mNGS confirmed the virus and supportive treatment led to full recovery (A5, A6, A7, A8, A9). Contribution: The report highlights key diagnostic clues differentiating hantavirus infection from pancreatitis and demonstrates the utility of mNGS for early pathogen confirmation (A10, A11). Limitations: Only an abstract is provided; detailed data and broader context are not reported.

papers.title_zh: 病例报告:由首尔 正汉坦病毒 引起的 肾综合征出血热 伪装为重症急性胰腺炎:动态影像演变及mNGS病原体确认。

analysis_zh.background: 肾综合征出血热(HFRS)是一种由 正汉坦病毒es 引起的动物源性疾病,表现为发热、血小板减少、肾功能受损和毛细血管漏出(A1)。其非典型表现可高度模拟急性胰腺炎,导致诊断困难(A2)。
analysis_zh.methods: 对一名33岁男性进行评估,初始及增强CT扫描显示胰腺周围、肾周围及后腹膜渗出(A4,A6)。进行全血宏基因组下一代测序,检测到高拷贝首尔病毒 正汉坦病毒(A7)。

papers.title: Early warning indicators for severe hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome.
papers.abstract: Hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) remains a significant public health concern, and early identification of severe cases is critical for improving outcomes. This review synthesizes recent advances in early warning indicators for severe HFRS. Clinically accessible indicators form the basis of early risk stratification. Key bedside signs such as high fever, severe gastrointestinal symptoms, altered mental status, and overt bleeding tendency, together with routine laboratory parameters including thrombocytopenia, leukocytosis, and elevated procalcitonin, have consistently shown robust predictive value for disease severity and mortality. Immunological markers provide mechanistic insight that also supports early identification of severe HFRS, as reflected by a core cytokine imbalance, impaired antigen-specific T- and B-cell responses, and aberrant activation of monocytes, neutrophils, and the complement system. Emerging biomarkers of endothelial barrier disruption, early renal tubular injury, oxidative stress, and metabolic dysregulation may further enhance predictive capacity. Despite these advances, challenges remain regarding external validation and clinical translation. Future research should focus on establishing standardized, multicenter-validated early warning systems to enable precise management of severe HFRS.

papers.full_text: AbstractHemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) remains a significant public health concern, and early identification of severe cases is critical for improving outcomes. This review synthesizes recent advances in early warning indicators for severe HFRS. Clinically accessible indicators form the basis of early risk stratification. Key bedside signs such as high fever, severe gastrointestinal symptoms, altered mental status, and overt bleeding tendency, together with routine laboratory parameters including thrombocytopenia, leukocytosis, and elevated procalcitonin, have consistently shown robust predictive value for disease severity and mortality. Immunological markers provide mechanistic insight that also supports early identification of severe HFRS, as reflected by a core cytokine imbalance, impaired antigen-specific T- and B-cell responses, and aberrant activation of monocytes, neutrophils, and the complement system. Emerging biomarkers of endothelial barrier disruption, early renal tubular injury, oxidative stress, and metabolic dysregulation may further enhance predictive capacity. Despite these advances, challenges remain regarding external validation and clinical translation. Future research should focus on establishing standardized, multicenter-validated early warning systems to enable precise management of severe HFRS.Keywords: biomarkers, early warning indicators, hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome, risk stratification, severe HFRS Supplementary materialThe Supplementary Material for this article can be found online at: https://www.frontiersin.org/articles/10.3389/fimmu.2026.1986264/full#supplementary-material Supplementary Materials 5.Conclusion and discussionHFRS severity progression is characterized by acute onset and rapid deterioration, and given the lack of specific antiviral therapy currently available, early identification of high-risk patients is critical for improving prognosis. This review addresses this core clinical challenge by comprehensively synthesizing predictive evidence from three dimensions, namely routine clinical indicators, immune dysregulation-related markers, and emerging biomarkers. It delineates the knowledge landscape of HFRS severity prediction.Bedside indicators and routine clinical parameters offer the greatest accessibility and constitute the foundation of the warning system. Expert Consensus has identified high fever, severe gastrointestinal symptoms, altered mental status, conjunctival chemosis, and obvious bleeding tendency as severity warning indicators (10). Pleural effusion and qSOFA score also provide independent warning information (19). Among laboratory indicators, thrombocytopenia and leukocytosis represent the most classic combination for early warning (11, 22). PCT demonstrates robust predictive value for severity and mortality (27), while CRP has limited independent predictive value (28). Elevated D-dimer and sTM reflect early hyperfibrinolysis and endothelial injury (23, 31). APRI and ferritin add warning information from the perspectives of hepatic injury and inflammatory burden (7, 40). Building on these indicators, multi-marker prediction models have been shown to substantially improve discriminative performance, highlighting the integration of multidimensional indicators as an effective strategy for enhancing the early warning capacity for severe HFRS (39, 41–43).Immunological markers also play a critical role in HFRS severity prediction. The elevation of IL-6 and TNF-α combined with the decrease of IFN-γ and TGF-β constitutes the core cytokine imbalance signature (49, 50, 52–54). Aberrant upregulation of MCP-1 and CXCL10 reflects excessive innate immune activation (56, 57). At the T cell level, attenuated antigen-specific responses and abnormal expansion of CD4+CD8+ T cells provide warning signals of severe HFRS (64). Delayed IgG responses are also a characteristic feature of severity (71). sCD163, as a monocyte-macrophage activation marker, is positively correlated with renal injury and negatively correlated with PLT, suggesting its potential in the prediction of severe HFRS (74).Emerging biomarkers extend the early warning capacity by encompassing pathophysiological dimensions that conventional measures do not completely cover, including endothelial injury, renal tubular injury, oxidative stress, and metabolic dysregulation. Severe AKI can be predicted by CysC and uNGAL prior to a noticeable elevation in Cr (93–95). sVCAM-1 and sCD138 can reflect the degree of vascular barrier injury, hinting at the potential for severe HFRS (85, 104). SOD and other oxidative stress markers, along with APN and resistin, provide additional warning signals from the perspectives of antioxidant defense and lipid metabolism disruption (98, 99, 101).Each category of biomarkers has its own strengths and limitations. Bedside signs and routine clinical parameters offer strong accessibility and reproducibility, but they often show abnormalities only when organ damage is already present. Immunological markers can provide earlier insight into severe warning, but their measurement often relies on specialized detection platforms such as flow cytometry and ELISPOT. Emerging biomarkers expand the scope of early warning, however, most of them remain at the single-center exploratory stage, and their independent predictive value and clinical feasibility still need further validation.Despite the relatively abundant evidence summarized above, the current literature on severe HFRS prediction still has several limitations. First, heterogeneity in study design remains the most critical barrier to the clinical translation of biomarkers in severe HFRS prediction. Most existing studies on early warning of severe HFRS consist of single-center retrospective cohort studies with small sample sizes, and there has been significant variation in inclusion and exclusion criteria, timing of biomarker measurements, and data collection methods. Although this design is reasonable under resource constrained conditions, its limitations are equally evident. Single-center data are deeply linked to the patient composition, clinical protocols, and laboratory capacity of the local hospital, so cutoffs derived in one institution may not be transferable to other regions. Single-center designs also make it difficult to effectively control the timing of sample collection. Given the distinct clinical phases of HFRS, the significance of a given biomarker may differ substantially between different stages. Furthermore, small sample sizes tend to introduce optimistic bias during the screening of candidate markers, and internal validation by itself cannot reliably indicate how a predictive model will perform in a different population (108, 109).Second, the existing research provides insufficient coverage of special populations. HFRS can occur at any age, yet the majority of current studies have focused on adults, particularly young and middle-aged individuals. However, the elderly, children, pregnant women, and patients with underlying comorbidities constitute a substantial proportion of the affected population, and their clinical phenotypes, rates of disease progression, and outcomes differ markedly from those of the general adult patient. For example, older patients often have diminished renal functional reserve and a high prevalence of hypertension and atherosclerosis. Even when viral load and inflammatory intensity are not particularly high, they are more likely to progress rapidly to AKI and heart failure (110, 111). Children represent the opposite scenario. Their renal tubular compensatory capacity is strong, and although fever and gastrointestinal symptoms tend to be more prominent than in adults, the incidence and severity of AKI are generally lower (112). Pregnant women add further complexity, as placental hemodynamic changes and fetal considerations place their circulatory volume, coagulation system, and immune status in a unique and dynamically balanced state (113, 114). Given these marked differences, establishing dedicated subgroup cohorts for special populations and developing stratified or subgroup-specific early warning tools represents an important direction for improving the applicability of predictive models in clinical practice.Lastly, the limited accessibility of detection platforms and the lack of evidence for incremental value remain the principal barriers to clinical translation. Many promising markers, such as CD4+CD8+ T cells, nCD64, cfDNA and soluble syndecan-1, often depend on flow cytometry or other high-throughput platforms. These techniques are time-consuming and costly, making their routine use difficult in primary care settings. More importantly, most existing studies have only examined associations between these markers and clinical outcomes, and whether adding them to conventional indicators truly improves the warning capacity remains unclear. Future work should promote point-of-care testing by integrating markers such as soluble CD163, cystatin C, nCD64, and procalcitonin into microfluidic, chemiluminescence, or immunochromatographic devices, shifting detection from central laboratories to the bedside. A tiered warning pathway should also be established, in which primary care institutions use routine indicators for initial screening, regional hospitals incorporate moderately accessible biomarkers for risk stratification, and large tertiary hospitals integrate immune and endothelial markers for refined management. Within this framework, prospective interventional studies are needed to determine whether biomarker-guided decisions can improve the accuracy of early warning of severe HFRS. Such evidence would clarify the incremental value of these markers and provide a solid foundation for their adoption in clinical practice. 1.IntroductionHemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) is an acute infectious disease caused by several Orthohantavirus species in the family Hantaviridae. Human infection usually occurs through inhalation of aerosolized virus from the excreta of infected rodents (1). The main causative viral strains differ by geographic region. Hantaan virus (HTNV) and Seoul virus (SEOV) are major causes of HFRS in Asia. HTNV infection may be associated with case fatality rates of approximately 5%–15%, whereas SEOV infection is generally milder. Puumala virus (PUUV) predominates in Europe and generally causes a milder form known as nephropathia epidemica (NE), with a case fatality rate of 0.1% to 0.4%. Dobrava virus (DOBV), which circulates mainly in the Balkans and other parts of Europe, has been documented to cause more severe disease (1–3). China accounts for >90% of the global HFRS burden, with more than 1.62 million cases and nearly 47,000 deaths from 1950 to 2014 (4). During 2014–2023, 91,388 total cases were reported, corresponding to an average annual incidence of 0.65/100,000 (5).Hantaviruses enter host cells primarily by binding to β3 integrins on the surface of endothelial cells (6, 7). Instead of directly lysing endothelial cells, viral infection initiates a strong innate and adaptive immune response, along with an inflammatory cascade. This results in endothelial barrier dysfunction, which can be clinically observed as increased vascular permeability, thrombocytopenia, coagulation disturbances, and acute kidney injury (AKI) (8, 9).Clinically, HFRS classically manifests five sequential phases: the febrile phase, hypotensive shock phase, oliguric phase, diuretic phase, and convalescent phase. Not all patients experience every phase in complete sequence; phase overlap frequently occurs, in which features of two or more phases appear simultaneously (10). HFRS can be classified into four grades: mild, moderate, severe, and critical. In clinical practice, mild and moderate cases are often grouped together as a broad “mild” category, while severe and critical cases are grouped as “severe” (7, 11–13). However, the criteria for severe disease are not fully consistent across different hantavirus infections. For HTNV infection, severe HFRS is defined by a body temperature >40 °C, neurological symptoms, shock, oliguria lasting ≥5 days or anuria lasting ≥2 days, or hemorrhage in vital organs (10, 14). For PUUV-induced nephropathia epidemica (NE), severe cases are often characterized by severe AKI or shock (15, 16). Despite these differences, the definitions all highlight the essential features of severe HFRS, including hypotension or shock, severe AKI, a significant bleeding tendency, and multiple organ dysfunction (17). Currently, no specific antiviral therapy is available, and the management of severe HFRS relies mainly on continuous renal replacement therapy (CRRT), mechanical ventilation, and vasopressor support (12, 17, 18). However, because of rapid progression to severe disease and the limited therapeutic window, intervention is often delayed, resulting in high mortality rates (14). Therefore, early recognition of patients at risk of severe progression and prompt initiation of intensive care are critical for improving outcomes.In recent years, research on early warning of severe HFRS has advanced considerably across multiple levels, encompassing bedside signs, routine laboratory parameters, immunological markers, and emerging novel biomarkers. In this review, we comprehensively synthesize progress in the aforementioned areas and evaluate the predictive performance and translational potential of various biomarkers. We also discuss current challenges and future perspectives, with the aim of establishing an evidence base for early identification and precise management of severe HFRS. 2.Clinically accessible warning systems for early risk stratificationClinically accessible warning systems including bedside signs and routine laboratory parameters are the most important indicators for predicting severe HFRS. This section reviews the available evidence on bedside signs and standard laboratory tests for predicting severe HFRS. The goal is to provide a practical framework for early risk assessment.2.1.Bedside signs of severe HFRS predictionBedside signs offer unique discriminative value for early risk stratification in HFRS, particularly in the absence of laboratory data. The 2021 Chinese Expert Consensus on Prevention and Treatment of HFRS identifies several key warning indicators for severe cases. These include a history of travel to endemic areas or contact with rodents and their excreta within two months prior to onset, high fever (temperature >40 °C or febrile duration exceeding one week), severe gastrointestinal symptoms such as intense nausea and vomiting, psychiatric disturbances including agitation or delirium, marked conjunctival edema, and obvious bleeding tendency (10). Regarding imaging findings, a retrospective analysis by Huang et al. of 191 patients with HFRS in southwestern China demonstrated that pleural effusion was an independent risk factor for progression to severe HFRS. Patients with pleural effusion had a 4.49-fold higher risk of severe progression compared to those without it, suggesting that this sign may reflect more extensive capillary leakage and systemic inflammation (14).The quick Sequential Organ Failure Assessment (qSOFA) score also has shown significant value in predicting severe HFRS. Ma and colleagues conducted a multicenter study of 551 HFRS patients in Hubei Province. They demonstrated that an admission qSOFA score of 2 or higher was an independent risk factor for 30-day mortality. The qSOFA score is defined as meeting any two of the following criteria: respiratory rate ≥22 breaths/min, systolic blood pressure ≤100 mmHg, or altered mental status. This finding suggests that the qSOFA score, without reliance on any laboratory tests, can serve as a rapid triage tool for early identification of high-risk HFRS patients and for determining the need for intensive care unit admission (19).Notably, the early warning indicators for severe HFRS vary across different age groups. Researchers at Tangdu Hospital have conducted stratified warning analyses for both older adults and children (20, 21). In the older-adult cohort (≥ 60 years), Li et al. reviewed 146 cases and identified several early warning signs using multivariate logistic regression. These included chest tightness or dyspnea, nausea or vomiting, decreased urine output (UO), skin and mucosal hemorrhage, and phase overlap (disease course spanning two or more typical phases). These findings suggest that assessment of older adults with HFRS should focus more on cardiopulmonary function, gastrointestinal symptoms, renal perfusion, coagulation status, and disease progression patterns (20). In the pediatric cohort (<16 years), the same group analyzed 103 cases. They found that conjunctival edema, hypotensive shock, and elevated serum creatinine (Cr) were key early warning indicators. This suggests that assessment in children should focus more on fluid extravasation, circulatory status, and early renal changes. Taken together, risk assessment should combine exposure history, consensus-based warning signs, bedside scores, and age-specific findings (21).2.2.Routine laboratory parameters for early warning of severe HFRS2.2.1.Blood cell indices and inflammatory markersBlood count and routine inflammatory markers are the most accessible laboratory indicators for evaluating the systemic host response in HFRS. Markedly elevated white blood cell count (WBC) and severely reduced platelet count (PLT) have long been recognized as warning signs for HFRS severity (11, 22). The 2021 Expert Consensus has established WBC >30 × 109/L and PLT <20 × 109/L as definitive severity warning thresholds (10). This pattern has been consistently confirmed by multiple retrospective cohort studies from various regions.
