SOD and other oxidative stress markers, along with APN and resistin, provide additional warning signals from the perspectives of antioxidant defense and lipid metabolism disruption (98, 99, 101).Each category of biomarkers has its own strengths and limitations. Bedside signs and routine clinical parameters offer strong accessibility and reproducibility, but they often show abnormalities only when organ damage is already present. Immunological markers can provide earlier insight into severe warning, but their measurement often relies on specialized detection platforms such as flow cytometry and ELISPOT. Emerging biomarkers expand the scope of early warning, however, most of them remain at the single-center exploratory stage, and their independent predictive value and clinical feasibility still need further validation.Despite the relatively abundant evidence summarized above, the current literature on severe HFRS prediction still has several limitations. First, heterogeneity in study design remains the most critical barrier to the clinical translation of biomarkers in severe HFRS prediction. Most existing studies on early warning of severe HFRS consist of single-center retrospective cohort studies with small sample sizes, and there has been significant variation in inclusion and exclusion criteria, timing of biomarker measurements, and data collection methods. Although this design is reasonable under resource constrained conditions, its limitations are equally evident. Single-center data are deeply linked to the patient composition, clinical protocols, and laboratory capacity of the local hospital, so cutoffs derived in one institution may not be transferable to other regions. Single-center designs also make it difficult to effectively control the timing of sample collection. Given the distinct clinical phases of HFRS, the significance of a given biomarker may differ substantially between different stages. Furthermore, small sample sizes tend to introduce optimistic bias during the screening of candidate markers, and internal validation by itself cannot reliably indicate how a predictive model will perform in a different population (108, 109).Second, the existing research provides insufficient coverage of special populations. HFRS can occur at any age, yet the majority of current studies have focused on adults, particularly young and middle-aged individuals. However, the elderly, children, pregnant women, and patients with underlying comorbidities constitute a substantial proportion of the affected population, and their clinical phenotypes, rates of disease progression, and outcomes differ markedly from those of the general adult patient. For example, older patients often have diminished renal functional reserve and a high prevalence of hypertension and atherosclerosis. Even when viral load and inflammatory intensity are not particularly high, they are more likely to progress rapidly to AKI and heart failure (110, 111). Children represent the opposite scenario. Their renal tubular compensatory capacity is strong, and although fever and gastrointestinal symptoms tend to be more prominent than in adults, the incidence and severity of AKI are generally lower (112). Pregnant women add further complexity, as placental hemodynamic changes and fetal considerations place their circulatory volume, coagulation system, and immune status in a unique and dynamically balanced state (113, 114). Given these marked differences, establishing dedicated subgroup cohorts for special populations and developing stratified or subgroup-specific early warning tools represents an important direction for improving the applicability of predictive models in clinical practice.Lastly, the limited accessibility of detection platforms and the lack of evidence for incremental value remain the principal barriers to clinical translation. Many promising markers, such as CD4+CD8+ T cells, nCD64, cfDNA and soluble syndecan-1, often depend on flow cytometry or other high-throughput platforms. These techniques are time-consuming and costly, making their routine use difficult in primary care settings. More importantly, most existing studies have only examined associations between these markers and clinical outcomes, and whether adding them to conventional indicators truly improves the warning capacity remains unclear. Future work should promote point-of-care testing by integrating markers such as soluble CD163, cystatin C, nCD64, and procalcitonin into microfluidic, chemiluminescence, or immunochromatographic devices, shifting detection from central laboratories to the bedside. A tiered warning pathway should also be established, in which primary care institutions use routine indicators for initial screening, regional hospitals incorporate moderately accessible biomarkers for risk stratification, and large tertiary hospitals integrate immune and endothelial markers for refined management. full_text_sections.other: 1.IntroductionHemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) is an acute infectious disease caused by several Orthohantavirus species in the family Hantaviridae. Human infection usually occurs through inhalation of aerosolized virus from the excreta of infected rodents (1). The main causative viral strains differ by geographic region. Hantaan virus (HTNV) and Seoul virus (SEOV) are major causes of HFRS in Asia. HTNV infection may be associated with case fatality rates of approximately 5%–15%, whereas SEOV infection is generally milder. Puumala virus (PUUV) predominates in Europe and generally causes a milder form known as nephropathia epidemica (NE), with a case fatality rate of 0.1% to 0.4%. Dobrava virus (DOBV), which circulates mainly in the Balkans and other parts of Europe, has been documented to cause more severe disease (1–3). China accounts for >90% of the global HFRS burden, with more than 1.62 million cases and nearly 47,000 deaths from 1950 to 2014 (4). During 2014–2023, 91,388 total cases were reported, corresponding to an average annual incidence of 0.65/100,000 (5).Hantaviruses enter host cells primarily by binding to β3 integrins on the surface of endothelial cells (6, 7). Instead of directly lysing endothelial cells, viral infection initiates a strong innate and adaptive immune response, along with an inflammatory cascade. This results in endothelial barrier dysfunction, which can be clinically observed as increased vascular permeability, thrombocytopenia, coagulation disturbances, and acute kidney injury (AKI) (8, 9).Clinically, HFRS classically manifests five sequential phases: the febrile phase, hypotensive shock phase, oliguric phase, diuretic phase, and convalescent phase. Not all patients experience every phase in complete sequence; phase overlap frequently occurs, in which features of two or more phases appear simultaneously (10). HFRS can be classified into four grades: mild, moderate, severe, and critical. In clinical practice, mild and moderate cases are often grouped together as a broad “mild” category, while severe and critical cases are grouped as “severe” (7, 11–13). However, the criteria for severe disease are not fully consistent across different hantavirus infections. For HTNV infection, severe HFRS is defined by a body temperature >40 °C, neurological symptoms, shock, oliguria lasting ≥5 days or anuria lasting ≥2 days, or hemorrhage in vital organs (10, 14). For PUUV-induced nephropathia epidemica (NE), severe cases are often characterized by severe AKI or shock (15, 16). Despite these differences, the definitions all highlight the essential features of severe HFRS, including hypotension or shock, severe AKI, a significant bleeding tendency, and multiple organ dysfunction (17). Currently, no specific antiviral therapy is available, and the management of severe HFRS relies mainly on continuous renal replacement therapy (CRRT), mechanical ventilation, and vasopressor support (12, 17, 18). However, because of rapid progression to severe disease and the limited therapeutic window, intervention is often delayed, resulting in high mortality rates (14). Therefore, early recognition of patients at risk of severe progression and prompt initiation of intensive care are critical for improving outcomes.In recent years, research on early warning of severe HFRS has advanced considerably across multiple levels, encompassing bedside signs, routine laboratory parameters, immunological markers, and emerging novel biomarkers. In this review, we comprehensively synthesize progress in the aforementioned areas and evaluate the predictive performance and translational potential of various biomarkers. We also discuss current challenges and future perspectives, with the aim of establishing an evidence base for early identification and precise management of severe HFRS. 2.Clinically accessible warning systems for early risk stratificationClinically accessible warning systems including bedside signs and routine laboratory parameters are the most important indicators for predicting severe HFRS. This section reviews the available evidence on bedside signs and standard laboratory tests for predicting severe HFRS. The goal is to provide a practical framework for early risk assessment.2.1.Bedside signs of severe HFRS predictionBedside signs offer unique discriminative value for early risk stratification in HFRS, particularly in the absence of laboratory data. The 2021 Chinese Expert Consensus on Prevention and Treatment of HFRS identifies several key warning indicators for severe cases. These include a history of travel to endemic areas or contact with rodents and their excreta within two months prior to onset, high fever (temperature >40 °C or febrile duration exceeding one week), severe gastrointestinal symptoms such as intense nausea and vomiting, psychiatric disturbances including agitation or delirium, marked conjunctival edema, and obvious bleeding tendency (10). Regarding imaging findings, a retrospective analysis by Huang et al. of 191 patients with HFRS in southwestern China demonstrated that pleural effusion was an independent risk factor for progression to severe HFRS. Patients with pleural effusion had a 4.49-fold higher risk of severe progression compared to those without it, suggesting that this sign may reflect more extensive capillary leakage and systemic inflammation (14).The quick Sequential Organ Failure Assessment (qSOFA) score also has shown significant value in predicting severe HFRS. Ma and colleagues conducted a multicenter study of 551 HFRS patients in Hubei Province. They demonstrated that an admission qSOFA score of 2 or higher was an independent risk factor for 30-day mortality. The qSOFA score is defined as meeting any two of the following criteria: respiratory rate ≥22 breaths/min, systolic blood pressure ≤100 mmHg, or altered mental status. This finding suggests that the qSOFA score, without reliance on any laboratory tests, can serve as a rapid triage tool for early identification of high-risk HFRS patients and for determining the need for intensive care unit admission (19).Notably, the early warning indicators for severe HFRS vary across different age groups. Researchers at Tangdu Hospital have conducted stratified warning analyses for both older adults and children (20, 21). In the older-adult cohort (≥ 60 years), Li et al. reviewed 146 cases and identified several early warning signs using multivariate logistic regression. These included chest tightness or dyspnea, nausea or vomiting, decreased urine output (UO), skin and mucosal hemorrhage, and phase overlap (disease course spanning two or more typical phases). These findings suggest that assessment of older adults with HFRS should focus more on cardiopulmonary function, gastrointestinal symptoms, renal perfusion, coagulation status, and disease progression patterns (20). In the pediatric cohort (<16 years), the same group analyzed 103 cases. They found that conjunctival edema, hypotensive shock, and elevated serum creatinine (Cr) were key early warning indicators. This suggests that assessment in children should focus more on fluid extravasation, circulatory status, and early renal changes. Taken together, risk assessment should combine exposure history, consensus-based warning signs, bedside scores, and age-specific findings (21).2.2.Routine laboratory parameters for early warning of severe HFRS2.2.1.Blood cell indices and inflammatory markersBlood count and routine inflammatory markers are the most accessible laboratory indicators for evaluating the systemic host response in HFRS. Markedly elevated white blood cell count (WBC) and severely reduced platelet count (PLT) have long been recognized as warning signs for HFRS severity (11, 22). The 2021 Expert Consensus has established WBC >30 × 109/L and PLT <20 × 109/L as definitive severity warning thresholds (10). This pattern has been consistently confirmed by multiple retrospective cohort studies from various…

analysis.background: HFRS is a major public health issue, and early detection of severe cases is vital.
analysis.main_directions: The review collates recent progress on early warning indicators for severe HFRS, covering clinical, immunological, and emerging biomarkers.
analysis.current_state: Clinically accessible indicators (bedside signs and routine laboratory parameters) currently form the basis of early risk stratification for severe HFRS.
analysis.gaps: External validation and clinical translation are limited; heterogeneity and single‑center retrospective designs hinder generalizability.
analysis.future_research: Standardized, multicenter‑validated early warning systems integrating multidimensional biomarkers are needed to enable precise management of severe HFRS.

analysis.summary_en: Background: HFRS is a major public health issue, and early detection of severe cases is vital. Main directions: The review collates recent progress on early warning indicators for severe HFRS, covering clinical, immunological, and emerging biomarkers. Current state: Clinically accessible indicators (bedside signs and routine labs) currently underpin early risk stratification. Gaps: Validation across settings and translation into practice remain limited, with heterogeneity and single‑center studies hindering generalizability. Future research: Calls for standardized, multicenter‑validated early warning systems integrating multidimensional biomarkers to improve precise management.

papers.title_zh: 严重肾综合征出血热的早期预警指标。

analysis_zh.background: 肾综合征出血热是重大公共卫生问题,早期发现重症病例至关重要。
analysis_zh.main_directions: 本综述汇总了近期关于重症肾综合征出血热早期预警指标的进展,涵盖临床、免疫学及新兴生物标志物。
analysis_zh.current_state: 目前,临床可获取的指标(床旁体征和常规实验室参数)构成重症肾综合征出血热早期风险分层的基础。

analysis_zh.future_research: 需要标准化、经多中心验证的早期预警系统,整合多维生物标志物,以实现对重症肾综合征出血热的精准管理。

papers.summary_zh: 背景：肾综合征出血热是重大公共卫生问题,早期发现重症病例至关重要。 主要方向：本综述汇总了近期关于重症肾综合征出血热早期预警指标的进展,涵盖临床、免疫学及新兴生物标志物。 研究现状：目前,临床可获取的指标(床旁体征和常规实验室参数)构成重症肾综合征出血热早期风险分层的基础。 不足：外部验证和临床转化有限;异质性以及单中心回顾性研究设计阻碍了结果的普适性。 后续研究：需要标准化、经多中心验证的早期预警系统,整合多维生物标志物,以实现对重症肾综合征出血热的精准管理。

papers.title: Andes virus molecular diagnosis and viral RNA kinetics using a research use only RT-PCR assay: Experience from a Spanish tertiary hospital.
papers.abstract: OBJECTIVES: To evaluate the clinical performance and qualitative agreement of a commercially available Research Use Only (RUO) real-time RT-PCR assay for Andes virus (ANDV) detection and longitudinal molecular monitoring during the first imported ANDV outbreak managed in Spain. METHODS: Fourteen repatriated individuals exposed to an ANDV outbreak underwent molecular screening using whole blood and serum specimens. Confirmed cases were prospectively monitored with serial whole blood, serum, oropharyngeal swab, urine, and rectal swab specimens collected every 72 h. Clinical specimens were inactivated in a Biosafety Level 3 facility before automated RNA extraction and testing with the RealStar® Hantavirus-HPS RT-PCR assay (Altona Diagnostics, Hamburg, Germany). All specimens were also analyzed at the Spanish National Reference Laboratory using a hantavirus-specific real-time RT-PCR reference method. Qualitative agreement, Ct value correlation, and viral RNA kinetics were assessed. RESULTS: A total of 185 clinical specimens were analyzed, including 124 screening specimens from exposed individuals and 61 specimens collected during longitudinal follow-up of two confirmed cases. All 124 screening specimens were negative by both assays (124/124, 100% agreement). Among follow-up specimens, overall qualitative agreement was 93.4% (57/61; κ=0.837), and Ct values showed a strong correlation between assays (Pearson's r = 0.965). Four discordant results occurred in specimens with high Ct values (≥34-35), consistent with low concentrations of detectable viral RNA. Whole blood showed the lowest Ct values and the longest persistence of detectable viral RNA among the specimen types evaluated. CONCLUSIONS: The RealStar® Hantavirus-HPS RT-PCR assay showed high qualitative agreement with the reference method in the clinical specimens evaluated and provided timely molecular information during outbreak investigation and longitudinal follow-up. Whole blood may be useful for longitudinal detection of ANDV RNA; however, these findings are descriptive and do not establish generalized viral shedding kinetics or infectivity. Further analytical and clinical studies are required to establish the assay's performance and clinical utility.

papers.title_zh: 安第斯病毒 分子诊断与病毒RNA动力学,使用仅限研究用途的RT-PCR检测:西班牙一家三级医院的经验。

analysis_zh.background: 本研究旨在评估用于 安第斯病毒(安第斯病毒)检测的研究用实时RT‐PCR检测的临床性能和定性一致性,并监测西班牙首次输入性安第斯病毒暴发期间的病毒RNA动力学。
analysis_zh.methods: 对14名因安第斯病毒暴发而被遣返的暴露者进行全血和血清筛查;对确诊病例进行前瞻性随访,按每72小时采集一次全血、血清、口咽拭子、尿液和直肠拭子标本。标本在BSL‐3实验室灭活,RNA自动提取,并使用RealStar® 汉坦病毒‐HPS RT‐PCR检测,同时在西班牙国家参考实验室使用针对 汉坦病毒 的参考RT‐PCR进行平行检测。评估了定性一致性、Ct值相关性以及病毒RNA动力学。
analysis_zh.contribution: RealStar® 检测与参考方法表现出高度定性一致性,并为暴发调查和纵向随访提供了及时的分子数据。全血可能有助于安第斯病毒RNA的纵向检测,尽管本研究为描述性结果,未能确立普遍的病毒脱落动力学或传染性。
analysis_zh.limitations: 本研究为描述性结果,未能确立普遍的病毒脱落动力学或传染性;需进一步的分析和临床研究以确认检测方法的性能和临床价值。

papers.title: Hantavirus as a catalyst for urgent One Health preparedness in Africa: strengthening the human-animal-environment interface.
papers.abstract: Hantavirus is a rodent-borne zoonotic pathogen that exposes critical gaps in global and African health preparedness at the human-animal-environment interface. Although historically linked to outbreaks in Asia, Europe, and the Americas, recent events, including a 2026 multi-country Andes virus cluster associated with international travel, underscore its epidemic potential and rare human-to-human transmission. In Africa, no large-scale indigenous outbreaks have been confirmed; however, ecological suitability, weak surveillance systems, and limited diagnostic capacity suggest possible under-detection. This commentary examines global preparedness systems and contrasts them with structural and operational gaps in Africa, including weak laboratory capacity, fragmented surveillance, and limited One Health integration. It also highlights implementation challenges, such as resource constraints and workforce shortages. Beyond technical systems, behavioral and social factors - including risk perception, community engagement, and trust - are essential to effective outbreak response. Strengthening One Health preparedness through laboratory investment, workforce training, regional collaboration, and community-based risk communication is essential to improving resilience against emerging zoonotic diseases.
